Defining Activation: The Aha Moment

Bengaluru, February 2024

On the morning of February 6, 2024, Meher Kohli, head of growth at the fintech app Kansya Pay, sat in front of a dashboard that told her two contradictory things at once. Downloads were up 41 percent month over month, driven by a cricket-season referral campaign paying ₹50 to each side when a friend joined. Thirty-day retention, however, had fallen from 19 percent to 14 percent. The board meeting was eleven days away, and the CEO wanted one slide that explained whether Kansya Pay was building a business or simply buying installs it would lose within a month.

Meher's funnel told her that 61 percent of new signups completed KYC, and of those, 88 percent linked a bank account. Both numbers had held steady for two quarters, so the growth team's usual explanation — that people were dropping off before they could experience the product — did not fit. People were finishing onboarding. They were still leaving. Something after the funnel's official finish line, and before the thirty-day mark, was determining who stayed and who quietly uninstalled. Meher had only a hunch, borrowed from a mentor at her previous job, that "there's an action in there somewhere that separates the users who stick from the users who churn." She was about to spend the next two weeks finding that action, and in doing so would rediscover, from first principles, a concept the industry calls activation.

The idea

Activation is the first meaningful use of a product — the point at which a new user has done something that lets them experience the value the product exists to deliver, as distinct from merely completing the mechanical steps of signing up. A user who has registered, verified a phone number, and set a password has completed onboarding. A user who has done the one thing that made the product's purpose real to them — sent a first message, completed a first paid transfer — has activated. Onboarding is administrative; activation is experiential. The distinction matters because onboarding completion is almost always poorly correlated with retention, while activation, properly defined, is one of the strongest predictors a product team has.

The term surfaced in its modern form inside the "pirate metrics" framework — Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, Revenue — that the venture investor Dave McClure popularized around 2007 to force startups to instrument the full customer lifecycle rather than obsessing over signups alone. McClure's insight was that founders knew how many people arrived and how much revenue came in, but had no vocabulary for the moment in between when a visitor became, functionally, a user. Growth teams at Facebook and Dropbox later sharpened the idea, discovering through cohort analysis that specific, countable early actions — the famous "seven friends in ten days" at Facebook, "one file in one folder on one device" at Dropbox — predicted retention far better than onboarding completion did. That refinement, the "aha moment," is what practitioners mean by activation today: not merely first use, but the specific first use that correlates with staying.

The single sentence Meher could say in the boardroom without sounding glib was this: "Activation is the first action a user takes that predicts they will still be here in thirty days — until we know what that action is, every acquisition number we report is a vanity number."

How it actually works

Finding an activation event is not guessing which onboarding step feels most important. It is an empirical exercise with a specific method, and the steps practitioners tend to skip separate a rigorous answer from a merely plausible-sounding one.

Step one: enumerate candidate actions

The team lists every discrete action a user could plausibly take early: for Kansya Pay, that meant completing KYC, linking a bank account, setting a savings goal, making a first peer-to-peer transfer, scheduling a recurring transfer, and inviting a contact. Onboarding steps belong on the list, but so do actions after onboarding formally ends — the mistake most teams make is treating the funnel's last screen as the natural place to stop looking.

Step two: define the retention outcome precisely

Before testing any candidate, the team fixes what "stayed" means and over what window. Meher chose "returned and completed at least one transaction in days 25–35 after signup" — a rolling window rather than a single-day snapshot, because a rigid "day 30 exactly" definition is noisy with a small cohort and easy to game with reminder notifications.

Step three: split users by whether they took each candidate action early, and compare retention

For every candidate, the team split new signups from the previous quarter into those who did the action within three days and those who did not, then compared their rates on the step-two outcome. This is the crux of the method: activation is measured as a correlation, not asserted, ideally across more than one cohort so a single lucky campaign does not masquerade as a durable pattern.

Step four: check the correlation is not simply "engaged users do everything"

The trap is circularity — highly engaged users complete more actions of every kind, so almost any candidate shows some lift. The discipline practitioners usually skip is checking whether the candidate lifts retention beyond what a generically active user would show anyway, for instance by comparing it against users who completed an equal number of unrelated actions. If the specific action still outperforms that baseline, it is a genuine signal, not enthusiasm.

Step five: make the definition falsifiable

"Used the app" is not an activation definition; it cannot be disproven. "Completed one peer-to-peer transfer of at least ₹100 within 72 hours" can be. The step practitioners skip is asking what evidence would prove their own definition wrong — if a cohort activates at a high rate by this definition but still churns, the definition is not yet right.

Fig. 1 — Onboarding completion (rust) stays flat and tells Meher nothing about who leaves. The retained-vs-activated split (green) shows the real divergence: users who transferred money early settle into a much higher plateau than the overall cohort.

A worked example

Meher pulled 4,000 signups from November 2023 and tested "completed a peer-to-peer transfer of ₹100 or more within 72 hours." Of the 4,000, 1,240 met that condition (31 percent) and 2,760 did not. She checked day-25–35 retention in each group.

GroupSignupsRetained (days 25–35)Retention rate
Transferred ≥₹100 within 72 hrs1,24052142.0%
Did not2,7602358.5%
All signups (blended)4,00075618.9%

The arithmetic is worth doing by hand once: 521 divided by 1,240 is 0.420, or 42.0 percent. 235 divided by 2,760 is 0.0851, or 8.5 percent. The blended rate, 756 divided by 4,000, is 18.9 percent — close to the 19 percent Meher had already been reporting, which is precisely the problem: the blended number hides a nearly five-fold gap between two very different populations. A user who transfers ₹100 in the first three days is roughly five times as likely to still be active a month later as one who does not.

Meher then ran a second pass, tightening the window to 24 hours, to see whether speed mattered as much as the action itself. Only 640 of the 4,000 signups transferred within 24 hours, and 301 were retained — 301 divided by 640 is 47.0 percent, three points above the 72-hour cohort's 42.0 percent. The remaining 600 who transferred between hour 24 and hour 72 retained at 220 divided by 600, or 36.7 percent — well above the non-transferring group's 8.5 percent, but below the fast movers. The activation event was not just "transfer ₹100" but "transfer ₹100 fast," and every day of delay cost the cohort measurable retention — a refinement a single pass never reveals, which is why a credible analysis re-cuts the data before calling a definition final.

The nuances a learner must become aware of

Activation is not the same as onboarding completion

Onboarding is what the product requires; activation is what the user experiences as valuable. A KYC form can be onboarding's final step and have zero relationship to whether the user returns, because filling in a PAN number delivers no value on its own — it merely clears a gate.

Correlation is not causation, and the direction can run backwards

It is tempting to conclude that transferring early causes retention, and that nudging everyone to transfer early will therefore raise retention. It may instead be that users who arrived already intending to use Kansya Pay seriously — referred by a trusted colleague rather than a cricket-season ad — both transfer early and were always going to stay. Nudges can raise the activation rate without raising retention at all if intent, not the action, was the real driver.

One activation metric can hide several different user journeys

A marketplace or multi-sided product often has no single aha moment: a buyer activates by completing a purchase, a seller by listing an item and receiving an enquiry, and averaging the two into one number obscures both.

The activation window is a modeling choice, not a fact of nature

Seventy-two hours, twenty-four, seven days — none is objectively correct; each is chosen to match how quickly the product's value is realistically reachable, and a window that is too generous flatters a weak product by counting slow, half-hearted engagement as success.

An activation metric decays and must be re-validated

A definition that predicted retention well for a referral-acquired cohort may stop predicting anything once the channel shifts to paid ads with different user intent, so the step-three correlation should be re-run whenever the incoming-user mix changes materially.

Activation is confused with "time to value," a related but narrower idea

Time to value measures how quickly a user reaches the activation event; activation is the definition of which event that is. A team can shrink time to value to zero and still have chosen the wrong event to optimize for.

A single activation event can crowd out habit formation

Facebook's "seven friends in ten days" was later refined because one completed action does not guarantee a returning habit; some teams now track a separate early-habit event, such as three transfers within two weeks, since one aha moment does not always predict sustained use.

Activation cannot tell you why non-activators stayed away

The split shows what happened, not why — product friction, a missing trusted contact, or simple lack of need. It motivates qualitative research; it does not substitute for it. A newcomer should also ask what window validated a number, whether it beat a generic-activity baseline, how recent the cohort was, and whether it still holds for today's channels.

Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and early-stage versus scale

In a consumer app like Kansya Pay, activation is usually a single, fast, individually completed action, because the buying group is one person and the decision cycle is minutes. In a B2B product, activation is often collective and slower: a project-management tool used by a twelve-person team at a firm like Naad Systems might define activation as "three or more team members created a task within the first week," since a single user opening the app proves nothing about team adoption, and the value only exists once collaboration begins. In a marketplace, activation is typically defined twice, once per side, and the sides interact — a buyer's activation (a completed purchase) may depend on enough sellers having already activated (a completed listing), which is why marketplace teams often track a joint "liquidity" measure alongside the two individual definitions.

The difference between an early-stage company and a large one is mostly how much the definition is allowed to move. An early-stage team should expect its activation hypothesis to be wrong more than once and re-run the step-three correlation every few months as the product changes. A large, mature company can afford a more rigid, board-reported metric, but pays a real cost if it fails to notice the metric has quietly stopped predicting retention as its user base and competitive landscape shift underneath it.

Common mistakes

Mistake one: treating the last onboarding screen as the activation event by default. The symptom is a dashboard where "activation rate" and "onboarding completion rate" are almost identical every week; the error is never having tested the correlation with retention. The cheapest diagnostic is the split Meher ran in step three — if it has never been run, the dashboard number is a guess wearing a metric's clothing.

Mistake two: picking an activation event that is too easy to hit. The symptom is an activation rate above 80 or 90 percent coexisting with poor retention. The error is defining activation as an action nearly everyone takes regardless of intent, so it carries no discriminating power. The cheapest diagnostic is checking whether the "did not activate" group is embarrassingly small.

Mistake three: optimizing the activation metric directly instead of the retention it predicts. The symptom is activation climbing while thirty-day retention stays flat or falls. The error is pushing users toward the event through prompts and incentives rather than making the value easier to reach, so users technically activate without finding the product useful. The cheapest diagnostic is re-running the correlation on the most recent cohort rather than trusting last year's number.

Mistake four: using one activation definition across genuinely different segments. The symptom is a healthy blended rate masking a segment that is quietly failing. The error is skipping the segmentation a marketplace or multi-persona product requires. The diagnostic is re-running the split separately within each major segment before reporting one company-wide number.

What good looks like

At Dhwani Fintech, a UPI-based savings app roughly Kansya Pay's size, the growth lead ran the five-step method before presenting any activation number to her board: she enumerated eleven candidates, fixed a rolling retention window, screened out the ones that merely tracked overall engagement, and settled on "created a named savings goal and funded it with at least ₹500 within five days" only after that action beat every generic-activity baseline. She then re-ran the test quarterly as her acquisition mix shifted from referrals toward paid search, caught a fifteen-point drop in the correlation's strength within two quarters, and adjusted the definition before it stopped meaning anything. That discipline — treat the definition as a hypothesis, not a fact — is what separates a team that uses the word "activation" correctly from one that has simply installed the word into its dashboard.

Closing

Meher presented the board with the transfer-within-24-hours definition, the 47.0 versus 8.5 percent split, and a plan: redesign the post-KYC screen to route every new user toward a first transfer with a trusted contact within a day, rather than toward the referral-sharing screen the growth team had previously prioritized. She was explicit that this was a hypothesis to be re-tested, not a settled fact, and committed to rerunning the split quarterly as the paid-acquisition channel grew. The board approved a narrower, less flattering growth number for the next quarter — activated users rather than raw installs — because it was the number that predicted the business Kansya Pay actually needed to build.

The next concept worth studying from here is cohort analysis: a single activation split, run once, is a photograph, while cohort analysis turns repeated snapshots into a moving picture of whether a product is getting better at converting signups into lasting users. From there, activation and onboarding optimization asks the harder design question: once you know the aha moment, how do you rebuild the product's first hour so more people reach it.

Two questions to sit with: First, if your product's most-quoted activation metric has never been checked against a generic-activity baseline, what is the chance it measures enthusiasm rather than what actually predicts retention? Second, how would you know, before your next board meeting, that your activation definition has quietly stopped working?

Purza Auto Parts: Which First Order Counts?

Chennai, September 2025. Before ₹6 crore of festive spending is committed, a product head must decide what a new garage has to do for Purza to call it a customer.

1. The Tuesday before the plan freezes

At a quarter past eight on the evening of Tuesday, 9 September 2025, Revathi Anand was the last person on the fourth floor of Purza Auto Parts' office in Guindy, Chennai. On her screen was a single slide titled "Activation — proposal", and it was empty except for the title. On 19 September, ten days away, Purza's leadership would lock the festive-quarter plan: ₹6 crore of marketing spend aimed at bringing independent car and two-wheeler garages onto Purza between Navratri and the end of December, the season in which Indian vehicle owners service their vehicles before the long drives home.

Revathi, Purza's head of product, had been asked to supply one number that the plan would be judged against. Not gross merchandise value — the board already had that. The chief executive's request had been narrower and harder: "Tell me what a garage has to do in its first month for us to say we have won it. Then we will spend the six crore on making that happen." She had ten days, four candidate answers, and a team that disagreed across five time zones.

2. Purza Auto Parts

Purza sold spare parts — brake pads, filters, belts, clutch plates, batteries, lubricants, and some 62,000 other stock-keeping units — to independent multi-brand garages: the two-bay and four-bay workshops that service cars and two-wheelers once they leave the authorised-service-centre network of Maruti Suzuki, Hyundai, Tata Motors, Mahindra, Honda and, increasingly, Ather and Ola Electric. Founded in Chennai in 2020 by two former distribution managers, Purza had begun as a WhatsApp order desk and become an app. A garage owner photographed a part or searched a catalogue, placed an order before 4 p.m., and received it the next morning from one of Purza's four warehouses in Chennai, Hosur, Coimbatore and Hyderabad.

By August 2025, 41,000 garages had registered on Purza, about 9,200 of them ordered in a given month, and monthly gross merchandise value stood at ₹18.4 crore. The company took a margin of roughly 11 per cent. GST e-invoicing had, unexpectedly, been a tailwind: garages that had to raise compliant invoices found Purza's automatically-generated documents easier than their distributor's handwritten challans. Payments ran on UPI and on a Razorpay-powered credit line for garages with three months of order history. ONDC's automotive category had opened a second discovery channel, and Amazon and Flipkart sold the same parts to the same garages, generally cheaper on small orders and unreliable on the fast-moving lines that a workshop cannot afford to be out of.

Purza's team had grown outward from Chennai. Its engineering was split between Bengaluru and Pune; its design lead, Aditi Bhaskar, worked from Berlin, where she had moved with her partner in 2023; its data science sat with Farhan Qureshi in Toronto; its customer-success organisation was run from Singapore by Priya Menon, who also held Purza's only substantial overseas account, Deira Auto Services, a nineteen-workshop chain in Dubai that had licensed Purza's catalogue software for ₹1.9 crore a year.

3. The situation

The trouble had surfaced in July. Purza's growth team was rewarded on new garages acquired and on the share of them that placed a first order. Both numbers were excellent: acquisition cost had fallen to ₹1,150 per registered garage, and 46 per cent of new garages placed an order within thirty days, up from 31 per cent a year earlier, largely because of a ₹500 first-order discount and a field team that helped owners place the order on the spot.

And yet the month-three numbers had not moved at all. Of garages that registered in April 2025, 22 per cent placed an order in July. Of garages that registered in April 2024, 21 per cent had placed an order in July 2024. Purza was acquiring more garages, converting more of them to a first order, and ending up with almost exactly the same proportion of live customers ninety days later. Somewhere between "placed a first order" and "is a customer", a large number of garages were quietly going back to their distributor.

Farhan, in Toronto, had spent three weeks on the data and had circulated his findings at 2 a.m. Chennai time on 2 September. His central table is reproduced as Exhibit 2. His conclusion was blunt: the first order predicted very little, and Purza had been optimising a metric that mostly measured whether the field team had been in the garage that week.

4. The people

Karthik Subramanian, VP Growth, Bengaluru. Karthik had built the acquisition engine and was measured on registered garages and first-order conversion. He argued that the existing definition was fine and the problem lay downstream in fulfilment. His practical objection to any stricter definition was timing: a metric that took twenty-one days to resolve could not steer a festive campaign in which a bad week had to be corrected in three days.

Farhan Qureshi, Lead Data Scientist, Toronto. Farhan wanted the definition with the largest separation between stayers and leavers, which his analysis said was a repeat order plus a saved parts list. He conceded, when pressed by Revathi on a late-night call, that he could not prove the action caused retention rather than merely revealing it.

Nisha Pillai, COO, Hosur. Nisha owned the warehouses and the fill rate, and she was the person with most to lose. If activation were defined as a first order delivered complete and on time, her operation became the owner of Purza's most important growth metric overnight, at a moment when festive volumes would already be straining the Coimbatore warehouse. Her stated position was that the definition should not depend on operations. Her unstated concern was headcount: she had asked for eleven more pickers and been given four.

Priya Menon, Head of Customer Success, Singapore. Priya saw the problem from her accounts. Deira Auto Services in Dubai had renewed twice, and what its workshop managers valued was not the first order but the moment their own parts list lived inside Purza and their juniors could reorder without asking. She believed the same was true of a Coimbatore garage, and that Purza had never measured it.

Exhibit 1 — What 3,400 garages registered in April 2025 did next

StepGaragesShare
Registered on Purza3,400100%
Completed GST and workshop details2,89085%
Placed a first order within 30 days1,56446%
First order delivered complete, on time1,00029%
Placed a second order within 21 days of the first61218%
Saved a parts list of 5+ SKUs47614%
Ordered in July (month 3)74822%

Source: Purza order database, extracted 1 September 2025. "Complete, on time" means every line item delivered by 11 a.m. the next working day with no substitution and no return raised within 72 hours. Note that 748 garages were live in month three while only 612 placed a second order within 21 days, so the two populations are not nested.

Exhibit 1 shows where the 46 per cent that Karthik's team celebrated actually leads. Of 1,564 first orders, 564 arrived late, short or wrong — a 36 per cent failure rate that nobody in the growth review had ever seen, because fulfilment quality was reported as a warehouse fill rate of 94 per cent, computed on lines shipped rather than on orders received intact by a garage.

Exhibit 2 — Month-three ordering, by what a garage did in its first 30 days

Early action in first 30 daysCoverageOrdered in month 3Did not do the actionLift
Completed GST and workshop details85%24%11%+13 pts
Placed a first order46%33%13%+20 pts
First order complete and on time29%49%11%+38 pts
Second order within 21 days18%71%11%+60 pts
Saved parts list of 5+ SKUs14%76%14%+62 pts

Source: Farhan Qureshi, analysis of the April 2025 registration cohort, 2 September 2025. Lift is the difference in month-three ordering between garages that did and did not perform the action; it is an association, not a measured causal effect. Coverage is the share of all 3,400 registrations.

Exhibit 2 is the heart of Revathi's problem. Reading down the table, lift rises steadily as coverage falls. The actions at the bottom — the second order, the saved list — separate stayers from leavers almost perfectly, and reach one garage in seven. The action at the top reaches almost everyone and tells you almost nothing. The first order, Purza's current metric, sits in the uncomfortable middle, and its +20 points conceal the split visible in the third row: a first order that worked is worth 49 per cent month-three retention, while the pooled figure of 33 per cent is dragged down by the 36 per cent of first orders that failed.

5. The options

Option A — keep "first order placed within 30 days". It is instrumented, understood by the field team, resolves in a day, and covers 46 per cent of registrations. Karthik favours it. Its cost is that Purza already knows it does not predict much, that the ₹500 discount inflates it, and that a festive quarter run on this metric will produce a record number of first orders in December and a flat month-three cohort in March, exactly as last year.

Option B — adopt "second order within 21 days of the first". This is the strongest honest predictor Farhan can offer, at 71 per cent month-three ordering against 11 per cent. Its cost is threefold: it covers only 18 per cent of registrations; it takes up to fifty-one days to resolve, which is most of the festive quarter; and it is close to the outcome it is meant to predict, so it may simply be retention wearing an earlier date.

Option C — adopt "first order delivered complete and on time within 48 hours". Coverage of 29 per cent, lift of 38 points, and resolution in three days. Its cost is political and operational: it makes Nisha's warehouses the owner of the growth metric during Purza's heaviest quarter, it requires the fill-rate definition to be rewritten from lines shipped to orders received intact, and it will make Purza's activation rate fall on the day it is adopted, from 46 per cent to 29 per cent, in front of a board that has been told the number was rising.

6. Questions for discussion

1. Using Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 2, what exactly has Purza been measuring with its 46 per cent first-order conversion, and why did improving it not improve month-three retention?

2. Exhibit 2 shows that the saved parts list has the highest lift of any action. What would have to be true for Purza to make it the activation metric — and what is the most likely reason its 62-point lift would shrink if Purza started pushing garages to create lists?

3. Nisha argues that activation should not depend on operations. Is she right in principle, and what does her position imply about who is allowed to own a growth metric?

4. Which option should Revathi take to the 19 September review, what would she measure to know within six weeks whether she chose correctly, and what would she ask the chief executive to stop reporting?

7. A note for the learner

The lens here is the definition of activation: the earliest observable action, within a stated window, that separates users who stay from users who leave. Purza's difficulty is the standard one. The actions with the largest separation are the ones a user only takes once they have already decided to stay, and the actions a team can easily move are the ones that separate nothing. A good answer navigates between them using three tests: does it predict (lift), can we reach enough people (coverage), and can the company cause it (moveability). Option B wins the first test and loses the third; Option A wins the third and loses the first.

One defensible path is Option C, with a specific structure around it. Revathi adopts "first order delivered complete and on time within 48 hours" as Purza's activation definition for the festive quarter, because it is the only candidate that is simultaneously decisive (+38 points), reachable (29 per cent today, with an obvious ceiling at 46 per cent if every first order simply worked), and caused by something Purza controls. She keeps the second-order-in-21-days rate as a validating metric reported monthly, not as a target: if activation rises and the 21-day repeat rate does not follow within two cohorts, the definition is wrong and she says so. She asks that the ₹500 discount be tested with a holdout in one region, because a discount that buys first orders Purza cannot fulfil converts marketing money into disappointed garages. And she takes the fall in the headline rate to the board herself, framed as a change of accounting rather than a decline, with Exhibit 1's 36 per cent failed-first-order figure as the evidence.

That path is defensible, not uniquely correct. A reader who argues for Option C in Chennai and Coimbatore while holding Option A in newly opened Hyderabad, where fulfilment is not yet stable enough to be a fair test, is reasoning well. So is a reader who insists on fixing the fill-rate definition before any activation metric is chosen at all.

Parchi Technologies: The Night Before the Board

Hyderabad, November 2025. Three parts of one company have three different answers to the question of when a customer has actually started using the product — and each answer pays someone differently.

1. Sunday, 16 November 2025

Meenal Kaushik had been in the Gachibowli office since eleven that morning, which was unusual for a Sunday, and by nine in the evening she had reduced the board deck from forty-one slides to nineteen and had still not written slide six. Slide six was titled "FY27 operating metric: activation", and beneath the title were three bullet points she had written and deleted four times.

The board met at ten the next morning. Two of the five directors would join from Singapore and Mumbai; the lead investor's partner would be in the room. What they had asked for, in an email sent eleven days earlier, was simple on its face: one definition of an activated customer, applied consistently, against which Parchi's FY27 plan and its growth spending would be measured. "We are being shown four different activation rates in four different documents," the partner had written, "and they range from 29 per cent to 67 per cent. Please pick one."

Meenal had spent those eleven days discovering that the four numbers were not four measurements of the same thing. They were four different beliefs about what Parchi sold, held by people in Hyderabad, Bengaluru, Pune, Berlin, Toronto, Singapore, New Jersey and Dubai, each of whom had built something on top of their belief — a contract, a commission plan, a machine-learning model, a spreadsheet, a renewal forecast — and none of whom was wrong in a way she could demonstrate.

2. Company history, and the decision that still binds

Parchi Technologies was founded in Hyderabad in 2019 by Meenal and Aniruddh Saraf, who had both worked in the finance function of a listed IT services company and had watched the same ritual every month: employees returning from client sites with pockets of paper slips — parchis — and a finance team spending nine days stapling, matching and arguing. Parchi's first product was straightforward software at ₹149 per employee per month: photograph the slip, the policy engine checks it, the approver approves on a phone, the entry lands in Tally or Zoho Books or SAP.

The decision that constrains everything today was taken in April 2022. Growth in seat-based SaaS was steady but slow, and competitors, some backed by far more capital, were giving the software away and earning on the card instead. Parchi followed. It signed a five-year exclusive card-issuing arrangement with Rohini Bank, a mid-sized private bank looking for commercial card volume, under which Parchi issued corporate cards to its customers' employees and kept 0.42 per cent of spend net of costs. The economics were transformative: by FY25, interchange was ₹58 crore of Parchi's ₹96 crore of revenue, against ₹38 crore of software subscriptions.

The contract came with a covenant. Parchi committed to a minimum of 6,000 newly activated cards per quarter, where the bank's definition of an activated card — written into Schedule 3, and not negotiable without reopening the whole agreement — was a first point-of-sale or online transaction within sixty days of issue. Below 6,000, Parchi paid a shortfall fee of ₹1.8 crore for the quarter. Parchi had paid it once, in the September quarter of 2023, and had never paid it again, because from that quarter onwards "first swipe in sixty days" became the number that the whole company watched.

It is worth being precise about what that meant. The metric did not come from Parchi's understanding of its users. It came from a bank's risk and revenue model, and it entered Parchi's operating system because it was attached to ₹1.8 crore. Within two quarters it was on the wall in Hyderabad, in the sales commission plan, in the customer-success onboarding checklist, and in the weekly email to the founders.

3. The industry around Parchi

Parchi sold to Indian mid-market companies of between 200 and 3,000 employees: IT services firms in Hyderabad, Pune and Noida; pharmaceutical companies in Ahmedabad; D2C brands in Bengaluru and Gurugram; auto-component manufacturers around Chennai. It had 610 paying accounts and about 2.9 lakh employees invited onto the platform.

Its competitors were of three kinds. Large horizontal software vendors, including the Indian SaaS firms Zoho and Freshworks, sold expense modules bundled into suites and were cheap to add for a company already inside those ecosystems. A set of well-funded card-led challengers, backed by the same payments infrastructure that had made Razorpay and PhonePe household names, competed hard on interchange rebates. And at the low end, an increasing number of finance teams simply used UPI, a shared spreadsheet and a WhatsApp group, which cost nothing and worked adequately until a company crossed roughly 300 employees.

Regulation touched the product at three points. The RBI's rules on co-branded cards constrained what Parchi could put on the card face and how it could hold customer data, and any change to the card issuance or activation journey required Rohini Bank's written approval — typically six to eight weeks. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act had forced a rewrite of Parchi's consent flow in early 2025 and limited how long receipt images could be retained, which had the side effect of deleting some of the evidence an analyst would want in order to study early behaviour. And GST input-credit matching gave Parchi one of its strongest selling points: a correctly captured invoice was money back for the customer, which meant Parchi's value was highest for exactly the expenses employees found most tedious to photograph.

Parchi's exposure outside India was small but disproportionately visible. Gurpreet Chhabra sold from New Jersey into the US subsidiaries of Indian-owned firms. And Creek Line Contracting, a 2,400-employee construction and facilities group in Dubai, was Parchi's largest single account at ₹4.6 crore a year — roughly 4.8 per cent of revenue, on a contract due for renewal on 31 January 2026.

4. The situation in detail

The first sign that something was wrong arrived in March 2025, when three accounts declined to renew. All three had shown card activation above 80 per cent in their first ninety days. All three had been green on every internal dashboard for a year. In the exit conversations, two of the three said some version of the same thing: their finance teams had never stopped running the month-end close in Excel, so Parchi had become, in effect, a corporate card with an app attached, and a competitor had offered a better rebate.

In June, Ramya Iyengar's customer-success team in Singapore began keeping a manual spreadsheet of which accounts had ever completed a full month-end close inside Parchi. By October it covered 120 of the 610 accounts, and the pattern in it was stark enough that Ramya sent it to the founders (Exhibit 3).

In August, Tanmay Bose in Toronto built a propensity model to predict renewal from first-90-day behaviour. It reported an AUC of 0.86, and its top feature by importance was total card spend in the first ninety days. Meenal had asked, on 4 November, whether card spend in the first ninety days was a predictor of renewal or simply an early measurement of the thing being predicted. Tanmay had said he would come back to her. He had not yet come back to her.

In October, Farida Rahman, group finance controller at Creek Line Contracting, told Ramya that she would be running a competitive process before the January renewal. Creek Line's card activation stood at 91 per cent. Its employees had submitted 38,000 expenses in the past year. Farida's complaint was that her team still could not close a month inside Parchi because the system's multi-entity handling could not represent Creek Line's four free-zone entities, and so her controllers exported everything and reconciled in Excel anyway.

And underneath all of it lay a fact Devansh Rathi had mentioned in a Bengaluru engineering review on 6 November and which had not yet travelled: since the SDK v4 migration in October 2024, the receipt_uploaded event had not been firing on Android when the image exceeded five megabytes. Newer Android phones photographed receipts at eight to twelve megabytes by default. Nobody knew how many submissions had gone uncounted, or for how long, or whether it also affected the downstream expense_submitted event. Roughly 71 per cent of Parchi's employee users were on Android.

5. The people

Aniruddh Saraf, co-founder and CEO, Hyderabad. Position: Parchi should keep first-swipe-in-sixty-days as the company metric through FY27. Incentive: the Rohini Bank agreement comes up for renegotiation in March 2026, and a strong activation record is his leverage for a better interchange share. Not saying: he has had two exploratory conversations about a larger card partnership that would require the same metric, and he has not told Meenal.

Ramya Iyengar, Head of Customer Success, Singapore. Position: the only activation that predicts renewal is the finance team completing a month-end close in Parchi. Incentive: her team is measured on net revenue retention, and an account-level definition puts her function at the centre of the operating model. Not saying: in at least fifteen of the accounts marked "close completed" in her spreadsheet, a Parchi implementation consultant configured the policy engine and ran the first close for the customer.

Tanmay Bose, Staff Data Scientist, Toronto. Position: no hand-picked threshold is needed; score every account with the model and let customer success work the bottom decile. Incentive: the model is his only visible piece of work this year, and his manager in Hyderabad is two levels removed and eleven and a half hours away. Not saying: he has a strong suspicion that card spend is leaking the outcome into the model, and that without it the AUC falls to about 0.68.

Shalini Varma, Head of Design, Berlin. Position: Parchi has been measuring the employee and ignoring the buyer; the aha moment belongs to the finance controller the first time the system catches a policy violation she would have missed. Incentive: she has been arguing for a controller-facing redesign for three quarters and this is the argument that could fund it. Not saying: she has an offer from a Berlin company and will decide in December.

Devansh Rathi, VP Engineering, Bengaluru. Position: no metric should be chosen until instrumentation is rebuilt, which he estimates at six weeks of one squad. Incentive: a data-quality mandate protects his team from a quarter of feature commitments. Not saying: the SDK defect was introduced by his own platform team and was visible in error logs since December 2024.

Sanket Deshpande, Principal Engineer, Pune. Position: quietly, that the card ledger from Rohini Bank is the only trustworthy dataset Parchi has, because it is reconciled to money. Incentive: he owns the events pipeline and knows exactly how fragile it is. Not saying: he has already written a script that reconstructs submissions from server-side API logs, which would take three weeks to validate, and he has not offered it because the last time he volunteered a side project it became his job for a year.

Gurpreet Chhabra, SVP Sales, New Jersey. Position: keep the card metric, which his enterprise prospects understand and which makes Parchi look mature in comparison to smaller vendors. Incentive: his FY26 commission accelerator pays on "activated accounts", defined as 60 per cent card activation within ninety days, and has already been communicated to eleven account executives. Not saying: two of his largest FY26 deals were signed with a first-swipe target written into the implementation plan, which his team meets by distributing cards at the kick-off workshop and asking employees to make a small purchase in the room.

Farida Rahman, Group Finance Controller, Creek Line Contracting, Dubai. Position: Parchi's cards work and Parchi's software does not do the one thing she bought it for. Incentive: she must show her group CFO a competitive process before renewing anything above 1.5 million dirhams. Not saying: she would renew tomorrow if multi-entity close were on a committed roadmap, and she has not said so because she does not want to weaken her negotiating position.

7. Voices

8. The options as Meenal currently sees them

Keep the card definition. First transaction within sixty days, as in Schedule 3. It is audited, it reconciles to money, it protects the covenant and Aniruddh's negotiating position, and it leaves sales compensation untouched. It is also, on the evidence of Exhibits 3, 4 and 6, the weakest of the three at predicting whether an account will still be paying next year — and Parchi has spent two and a half years teaching its entire go-to-market organisation to produce it, including, in Gurpreet's accounts, by asking employees to buy something in a workshop.

Move to the employee submission definition. First expense with a receipt within fourteen days of invitation, reported as a share of invited employees. It is closest to what the software actually does, it is the definition most product teams would recognise, and it ranks the D2C segment correctly. It currently rests on an events pipeline that engineering says it cannot vouch for within ten points, it would show a headline rate of 29 per cent against the 67 per cent the board has been seeing, and it says nothing about the buyer.

Move to the account-level close definition. First month-end close completed inside Parchi within ninety days of go-live. It has the highest renewal association in Exhibit 4, it captures the buyer's job, and it would direct the roadmap towards the multi-entity work Creek Line is waiting for. It also exists only as a manually maintained spreadsheet covering a fifth of the customer base, it takes up to ninety days to resolve, it is satisfiable by a Parchi consultant doing the work on the customer's behalf — which Ramya's team has done at least fifteen times — and it would produce a denominator of new accounts per quarter small enough that the metric would be noisy from month to month.

Reading her own three paragraphs at half past ten, Meenal noticed something that made the slide harder rather than easier. Each option assumes that Parchi has one activation, one user and one moment. Exhibit 6 suggests it may have two products serving two different jobs; Exhibits 2 and 3 together suggest the employee and the controller succeed and fail independently; and Exhibit 1's footnote suggests that for one of the three candidates she does not currently possess the ability to measure the thing she would be committing the company to. She wrote a fourth bullet, looked at it, and deleted it.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets at ten on Monday, 17 November. Parchi holds ₹148 crore in cash with nineteen months of runway at the current burn, and the FY27 plan assumes a Series C conversation beginning in the September quarter of 2026. The Rohini Bank covenant requires 6,000 newly activated cards per quarter on Schedule 3's definition, with a ₹1.8 crore shortfall fee; the December quarter is tracking at 6,900. Any change to the card issuance or activation journey requires the bank's written approval, historically six to eight weeks. Renegotiation of the agreement opens in March 2026.

Engineering can commit one squad of six for six weeks in the December–January window, and only one: the same squad is the only one that can start multi-entity close, which Creek Line's ₹4.6 crore renewal on 31 January appears to depend on. The DPDP consent rewrite has already consumed the compliance budget for the year, and receipt images older than 180 days are deleted, which limits how far back any reconstruction of submission history can reach. Sales compensation for FY26 is contractually communicated and would cost approximately ₹40 lakh to restructure mid-year. Ramya has two open customer-success roles she has been unable to fill in Singapore at the approved salary band, which is 40 per cent below what the same role commands in her market.

10. Questions for discussion

1. Exhibits 1 and 2 cannot both be describing the same reality. List every explanation for the gap that is consistent with the footnotes, and say what single piece of evidence would most cheaply distinguish between them.

2. Exhibit 4 shows a 95 per cent renewal rate for accounts completing a month-end close. Name three reasons that number might mislead a reader who took it at face value, using only what the case tells you.

3. Parchi's company-wide metric was inherited from a bank's contract rather than chosen from an understanding of users. What does an organisation lose when its central operating metric has that provenance, and what, if anything, does it gain?

4. Exhibit 6 ranks the two segments in opposite orders depending on the definition used. Is a single company-wide activation definition defensible for Parchi at all? If not, what does Meenal put on slide six?

5. Consider the incentives described in section 5. For each of the three options, identify who would work to satisfy the metric without delivering the underlying value, and by what mechanism.

6. It is Monday morning. What does Meenal do — with the squad, with the covenant, with Creek Line, with Gurpreet's compensation plan — and what exactly does she say to the board about a number they have been shown for two years that she now believes is the wrong one?

At eleven twenty she made tea and came back to the desk. Sanket had sent a message from Pune at 10:58: "Meenal, I have something that might reconstruct submissions from the API logs going back to Jan 2025. Not validated. Three weeks if we commit someone. Only if useful." She read it twice. Three weeks was after the board, after the December quarter closed, and the only squad that could do it was the squad Creek Line was waiting for.

Slide six still said "FY27 operating metric: activation", and underneath it, now, there was nothing at all.

Metrics, Analytics & Experimentation · Product Analytics & Data Practice

Defining activation (the aha moment): the depth treatment

1. Two boards, two Septembers

On 9 September 2026, Ira Vaidyanathan, VP Product at Prajwalan Systems in Bengaluru, received a Series B diligence request with one line she could not answer honestly: "activation rate by cohort." Prajwalan sold an AI contract-review copilot to Indian law firms at ₹4,200 per seat per month across sixty-one accounts and 2,900 seats, and reported that 78 per cent of provisioned seats ran a document through review in week one. The onboarding wizard ended with a sample contract loaded and a large blue button; declining took effort. Ninety-day seat retention was 34 per cent, and a gate 78 per cent clear cannot explain which third stays. An August audit of 400 first reviews found 22 per cent returned output the user plainly could not use: in a probabilistic product, one run is a draw, not evidence of value.

Thirteen days later and 840 kilometres west, Nandita Rau, Chief Product Officer of Sphuling Health in Pune, faced the mirror image. Sphuling sold a ₹1,790 Bluetooth glucometer through pharmacy chains, gave the app away and earned on a ₹349-a-month coaching subscription, taking 214,000 installs in the year to August 2026. Reported activation — profile completed, one reading logged — was 43 per cent; ninety-day subscription retention was 11 per cent. Her annual plan, due at the 22 September board, rested on one assumption: that ₹6.2 crore spent lifting activation ten points would lift retention enough to pay for itself.

Both were approaching the same thing from opposite directions. An activation definition is not a discovery about users; it is a compressed claim about causation dressed as an observation, and the discipline consists of knowing how much of that claim the evidence supports.

2. The idea, and the four camps that disagree about it

An activation definition is a choice of action, window and threshold such that an organisation uses the resulting binary indicator as its stand-in for "this user has experienced the product's value"; the aha moment names the experience the event proxies. Three jobs hide inside that definition, and conflating them causes most disputes: activation can be a predictive marker, a causal lever, or an organisational contract dividing what growth owns from what product owns. The statistical requirements differ, and a definition excellent at one can be useless at another.

The lineage predates software: catalogue marketers tracked first-to-second-purchase conversion as the sharpest early signal in an RFM file, packaged-software firms trial-to-paid. Dave McClure's 2007 pirate metrics named the stage rather than discovering it, giving founders a word for the gap between arrival and habit. The 2010s growth teams supplied the method and, less helpfully, the folklore: Facebook's "seven friends in ten days," Dropbox's "one file in one folder," Slack's "two thousand messages." People close to those numbers have since said they were over-read — the Facebook figure was a correlate in one cohort at one time, and the Slack figure a team-level threshold saying almost nothing about an individual.

Four camps hold genuinely different positions. The predictive-marker school, dominant in growth analytics, holds that activation's value is as a fast, stable leading indicator: one definition, validated against retention, re-checked, reported to the board. It will not sign the claim that raising the rate necessarily raises retention.

The causal-lever school, out of the online-experimentation tradition, holds that a definition nobody has randomised is not yet a management object. It signs only events for which an encouragement experiment has shown a retention effect, and never an activation OKR on observational evidence.

The jobs-and-first-value school — Christensen's jobs-to-be-done crossed with the onboarding-design tradition of Kathy Sierra and Samuel Hulick — holds that where proxy and experience diverge you trust the experience. It signs a statistically weaker definition describing something a user would recognise as valuable, and will not sign an event chosen purely on correlation if no user would call it the moment the product became useful.

The intensity school, associated with power-user curves and the habit literature, denies there is a moment at all: what predicts retention is early frequency relative to the product's natural cadence, and any binary event is a lossy compression of a rate. It signs "three sessions in week one" over "did action X."

Behind all four sits a sceptical position: most of the gap is selection on pre-existing intent, so activation rate is a lagging measure of acquisition quality, and a team paid on it will improve it by buying better traffic.

3. Mechanics: choosing an event, and what the choice estimates

Most teams select on the wrong statistic: the candidate with the highest lift, the ratio of retention among takers to retention among non-takers. For a binary split with coverage p, retention r1 among takers and r0 among non-takers, the variance in the outcome explained by the split is

V = p(1 − p)(r1 − r0)2

This between-group variance penalises both failure modes: an event almost everyone takes has a tiny p(1 − p) and explains nothing even if the few refusers churn, while an event almost nobody takes has a huge gap and still explains nothing. Nandita's team scanned Sphuling's January–March 2026 cohort of 38,400 signups against a ninety-day outcome, any session in days 85–100. Blended retention was 14.2 per cent.

Exhibit 1 — Sphuling Health, Jan–Mar 2026 cohort, n = 38,400. Index = 1,000 × p(1 − p)(r1 − r0)2. Blended retention is 14.2% in every row; only the split differs.
Candidate event (within 14 days)CoverageRet. if yesRet. if noLiftIndex
Completed health profile86%15.2%8.1%1.9×0.61
Logged one reading63%19.7%4.9%4.0×5.11
Paired the device41%25.6%6.3%4.1×9.01

3 days & shared with family11%44.1%10.5%4.2×11.05
Started coach subscription6%59.6%11.3%5.3×13.16

Two readings separate a competent analyst from an expert. The highest-lift row, subscription start at 5.3×, also carries the highest index — and is disqualified, not by any statistic but because starting a subscription is nearly the outcome itself. The index cannot see circularity; a human must. Second, the winner on non-circular grounds beats device pairing by 40 per cent on explained variance while showing only a slightly better lift. Lift ranked the candidates almost randomly.

The second mechanic most teams never perform: activating requires surviving. A user who uninstalls on day three cannot log readings on three separate days in fourteen, so part of the 24.8-point gap is definitional. The epidemiological name is immortal time bias; the fix is a landmark analysis restricted to users still present at the window's end. Of Sphuling's 27,264 non-activators, 12,900 had gone dark before day fourteen and were never eligible; among the 14,364 present at the landmark, 1,760 were still there in days 85–100, or 12.3 per cent. The honest comparison is 31.8 against 12.3 — 19.5 points and 2.6×, not 4.5×.

The third mechanic decides whether the metric is a lever or only a marker. The landmark-adjusted gap is still observational: activators differ in intent, channel and condition severity, not only in whether they were nudged. Sizing the lever requires an encouragement design — randomise the nudge, not the behaviour. Sphuling ran one on 24,000 pharmacy-channel users, pairing-first flow against profile-first.

Exhibit 2 — Sphuling encouragement experiment, Apr–Jun 2026, n = 24,000. The complier average causal effect is the intention-to-treat effect divided by the compliance gain, valid only if the nudge affects retention solely through activation.
QuantityControlTreatmentDifference
Activation (3 readings / 14 days)28.6%41.4%+12.8 pp

Those three numbers — 24.8, 19.5, 10.9 — are the intellectual content of the topic. They measure the same relationship and differ by more than a factor of two, because each answers a different question: who differs, who differs once survival is held constant, and what changes if we intervene. On the raw gap, Nandita would have forecast 3.2 points of retention from a 12.8-point activation gain. It delivered 1.4, and the ₹6.2 crore would have been sized against the error.

Two mechanics stay implicit. The window trades predictive power against feedback latency: Sphuling's index peaked at fourteen days (12.66) but sat at 11.9 at seven — six per cent less power for half the reporting lag, a trade experienced teams often take deliberately. And the grid search is a multiple-comparisons problem. Nandita's team tested 34 events across six windows and four thresholds: 816 splits. The best in-sample index was 14.9; on the held-out 26,400 it fell to 12.66, and the fifth-ranked event in sample ranked first out of sample.

4. When the idea holds, and when it misleads

The conditions are testable claims. One: the product has a value moment reachable inside an actionable window. True at Sphuling — a first fortnight of readings is a real experience; contestable at Prajwalan, where value compounds across a matter running months. Two: the decision unit is the unit measured. True at Sphuling, where one person owns the condition and the device; false at Prajwalan, where renewal is decided by an account, often by a partner who never logs in.

Three: enough retention variance is attributable to experience rather than selection. Sphuling's experiment says yes, though less than half; Prajwalan is worse placed, since most seats are provisioned by an administrator rather than requested, so non-activation is often a fact about procurement. Four: the event is logged reliably and is not gameable by the team that owns it. This is the claim teams never write down and most often violate.

The idea actively misleads in three situations. Where natural frequency is very low — tax filing, insurance renewal, home loans — the gap to the next genuine occasion of use is so long that an early binary event predicts little, and forcing one measures enthusiasm. Where a product is sold top-down into enterprises, activation measures implementation progress product does not control. And where the acquisition mix shifts fast, activation moves for reasons unrelated to the product.

5. Hard edges: two-sided, hardware, regulated, multi-product, AI-native

Chingaara Commerce, a Jaipur handicrafts marketplace, defines buyer activation as a first order delivered and not returned within 21 days, seller activation as three photographed listings live plus one fulfilled order within 30 days. Cutting its 2026 cohort by district supply density shows what a blend conceals.

Exhibit 3 — Chingaara Commerce, 2026 cohort by district supply tier. Seller activation is roughly constant; buyer activation is a property of the district as much as the buyer.
District tier (active sellers)Seller activationBuyer activationBuyer 180-day retention
Liquid (> 400)38%31%42%
Thin (120–400)34%19%26%
Very thin (< 120)33%11%14%

A company-wide buyer activation rate at Chingaara mixes product quality with supply coverage, so a growth team paid on it will expand into liquid districts and avoid thin ones — the opposite of what the business needs. Mature marketplaces read activation within a liquidity tier and treat the company-wide figure as a mix report.

Sphuling's pharmacy channel introduces a physical act — unboxing and pairing — with a lag the app cannot observe. A device sold on 3 September may be opened on the 20th, so a window anchored to install is wrong for pharmacy and right for direct; Sphuling anchors instead to first launch on a paired serial. It also carries a "shipped, never paired" cohort invisible to the metric: 18 per cent of 2026 pharmacy units, the largest pool of lost value in the business, appearing in no funnel.

Deepan Grid in Chennai sells billing software to state distribution utilities. Logins are shared across control-room shifts, so user-level activation is uninterpretable, and the earliest genuine value is a production go-live at a median 194 days from contract. Deepan defines activation as the first billing cycle run end-to-end in production — an implementation milestone, which is the honest answer here and means the metric belongs to delivery, not product.

Multi-product companies define activation per product and roll it up. The second-order effect is a sequencing question nobody owns: activating on the easy product may consume the political capital needed for the hard one. Mature firms answer with an explicit landing-product policy and measure activation only there.

Prajwalan's edge is that one use of a probabilistic system is a draw, not an experience. Its audit put the in-session acceptance rate for suggested revisions at 0.44 in a first session and 0.71 by the fourth, as users learned to scope requests, so a one-shot definition penalises users who drew badly and flatters those who drew well — neither fact being about the product's value to them. Ira's candidate — one accepted or edited-and-kept revision in each of two separate sessions within ten days — covers 37 per cent of seats at an index of 11.2, against 78 per cent coverage and 2.3 for "ran one document." A review also costs roughly ₹38 in inference, so activation in AI products is not free to manufacture.

At the seams, mature companies say the definition is owned by data and reviewed annually; what they do is freeze it, because changing it breaks year-over-year comparisons, regrades last year's OKRs and reassigns headcount. The workable practice, run quietly at several large firms, is two numbers: a frozen reported activation for continuity and a research activation refitted quarterly, retiring the former if they diverge beyond a set margin for two consecutive quarters.

6. Nine things experts see that competent practitioners do not

The window manufactures part of the gap. The tell is a window long relative to the churn being predicted — thirty days against a sixty-day outcome. The obvious reading is that a generous window is charitable; the expert reading is that it guarantees activators survived a month while non-activators may not have survived a week. If nobody can state the gap among users alive at the window's end, the number has never been stress-tested.

Lift is the wrong objective. The tell is a slide quoting "activated users retain 6× better" with no coverage figure on it. The obvious reading is that a bigger ratio is a stronger finding; the expert reading is that ratio and coverage trade off. A 6× lift on a 4 per cent event describes a self-selected elite and gives the onboarding team nothing to build toward.

The observational gap is not the lever. The tell is a plan multiplying a projected activation gain by the observed gap. The obvious reading is a fair back-of-envelope; the expert reading is that it conflates being the kind of user who activates with being moved to activate, and the second is a fraction of the first — at Sphuling, 44 per cent. Such forecasts always overstate.

A definition chosen from a large grid is partly noise. The tell is an oddly specific definition — "four actions of type B within nine days" — arrived at without a holdout. The obvious reading is rigour; the expert reading is that eight hundred comparisons always produce a spuriously strong winner that regresses on fresh data.

Making it a target begins destroying it. The tell is a rate climbing steadily while the retention it was chosen to predict does not move. The obvious reading is that retention lags; the expert reading is Goodhart — the team found ways to produce the event without the experience, and the correlation has eroded since the quarter it became an OKR. The diagnostic is the correlation as a time series.

The unit of analysis is a decision, not a fact. The tell is per-seat activation where renewals are signed per account. The obvious reading is that seats aggregate; the expert reading is that multiplayer products have threshold effects — one enthusiast in a firm of forty predicts nothing, three colleagues on the same matter predict a great deal — so account-level definitions with a headcount condition beat the seat-level average.

Intent is the largest confounder, and it is channel-shaped. The tell is one rate quoted across referral, paid search and pharmacy-shelf acquisition. The obvious reading is that the blend is the company's rate; the expert reading is that intent varies more across channels than the product varies across users, so the blend is a mix report, and when it moves the first hypothesis is that the mix moved.

Proxies rot when the product changes. The tell is a definition written before a major redesign and never revisited. The obvious reading is stability; the expert reading is that the definition encoded a route to value through one interface, and a redesign can move the value moment without moving the event — leaving a metric stable because it has stopped tracking anything.

The definition is a political object. The tell is a data team that could produce a better definition in a week and has not proposed one in two years. The obvious reading is inertia; the expert reading is that the boundary between activation and retention is the boundary between two budgets, and moving it later moves headcount from growth to product. An expert makes the analytical and organisational cases together, or watches the analytical one lose.

7. How it differs by product type and by stage

In consumer products the definition is individual, fast and singular, and the main risk is an event that is too easy. In B2B it is multiplayer and the risk is measuring the wrong unit; the working rule is an account-level definition with a distinct-user condition, seat-level activation kept as a diagnostic beneath it. In enterprise, activation is honestly an implementation milestone owned by delivery. In marketplaces it is defined twice and read within a liquidity tier. In hardware-plus-software the physical act sits inside the window and outside the telemetry. In AI products value is a distribution, arguing for two successful episodes rather than one.

Stage changes less than practitioners expect; what changes is tolerance for revision. A pre-product-market-fit company should expect to be wrong repeatedly and refit quarterly, because nothing is built on the definition yet. A company at scale carries real switching costs — dashboards, OKRs, board narratives, compensation. What does not change with stage: the landmark correction, the explained-variance criterion and the observational-causal gap apply identically at twelve users and twelve million.

8. Three worked cases, one of them a failure

Tinkaar Learning, Lucknow. A vernacular upskilling app at ₹199 a month scanned 61,000 signups and chose "completed one lesson and returned on a second calendar day within 72 hours" — coverage 22 per cent, index 15.8 in sample, 14.9 out. An encouragement test moved activation from 22 to 31 per cent and day-60 retention from 9.8 to 11.3: an ITT of 1.5 points, an implied CACE of 16.7. Over three quarters activation reached 34 per cent and day-60 retention 12.4, against the 2.0 points the CACE predicted. The team reported the 2.6-point gain but declined to claim all of it as caused, a content expansion having shipped alongside.

Jwalan Freight, Nagpur — the failure. Jwalan sold transport-management software to fleet operators and defined activation as uploading a first consignment within seven days. A Q1 2026 campaign of in-app nudges plus a revised SDR script took activation from 31 to 58 per cent; over the next two quarters 120-day account retention fell from 47 to 41. The mechanism was specific: the forty minutes an SDR had spent mapping a customer's lanes and rate master were reallocated to securing the upload. Accounts uploaded a test consignment, hit wrong rates on the second real one, and stopped. The metric had been moved by removing the work that made it meaningful.

Recovery took three quarters. Jwalan re-ran the scan at account level and found the strongest non-circular definition was "two or more distinct users from the account created a consignment in the same week, within 21 days" — index 18.4 against 6.1. The configuration call was restored as a gate and retention recovered to 52 per cent. The detour cost roughly ₹2.6 crore of churned ARR, and throughout it the campaign looked like the most successful growth initiative in the company's history.

Chingaara Commerce, Jaipur. Chingaara's contribution is a negative result. It tested whether buyer activation in very thin districts could be lifted by onboarding alone: a curated first-purchase carousel, delivery guarantees, a ₹100 credit. Activation rose from 11 to 14 per cent while 180-day retention moved from 14.0 to 14.6, inside the confidence interval; in liquid districts the same treatment moved activation 31 to 36 and retention 42 to 45. Below a supply threshold, buyer activation is not a product problem — a conclusion an activation programme should reach and rarely does.

9. Failure modes, warning signs and the cost of late diagnosis

The tautological definition. Warning sign: activation and onboarding-completion move together to within a point every week. Diagnostic: what fraction of the cohort fails this event, and what happens to them? Caught late, a planning cycle is spent optimising a gate rather than an experience.

The unfalsified lever. Warning sign: a retention forecast derived by multiplying an activation gain by an observational gap. Diagnostic: has this event ever been randomised, and what was the ITT? Caught late, at the end of a funded programme, the shortfall is blamed on execution rather than the model, and the error repeats.

Metric capture. Warning sign: the rate rises four quarters running with no retention movement. Diagnostic: what is the correlation this quarter against when the definition was set? Caught late, the organisation has steered for years by an instrument that stopped reading.

Wrong unit. Warning sign: strong seat-level activation with weak account renewal. Diagnostic: who signs the renewal, and is that entity in the denominator? Caught late, the team has optimised the experience of someone who does not make the buying decision.

Instrumentation failure. Warning sign: a sharp discontinuity on the date of a client release. Diagnostic: did event volume change, or did the population? The cheapest failure to catch and the most embarrassing to catch late, because teams spend weeks investigating a behaviour change that was a logging change.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Is there a moment at all? The single-event camp argues that a binary definition is the only thing an organisation can coordinate around: legible, fits on a wall, a team can be asked to move it. Its evidence is that well-chosen events explain a substantial share of retention variance and that products with clear definitions ship more coherent first runs. The intensity camp replies that the reality is a frequency distribution, that binarising discards information, and that early-session-count models out-predict single-event models on most consumer datasets. For it to be wrong, organisations would have to act on a continuous score as effectively as a binary one — a claim about organisations, not statistics, and the single-event camp's strongest ground.

Causal or selection? The lever camp points to encouragement designs like Sphuling's: the relationship survives randomisation, so something in it is causal. The selection camp replies that a 1.4-point ITT is equally consistent with activation being a marker of intent with a thin causal margin, and that firms publish only wins. For it to be wrong, encouragement effects would need to hold across channels with very different intent profiles; that has rarely been tested.

One number or several? The single-number camp argues that a metric's value is largely coordinative, that three definitions is functionally zero, and that segment-specific definitions become unauditable. The segmentation camp points to Chingaara, where a company-wide rate misdirects investment. Both are right about different costs; the disagreement turns on whether coordination or measurement is currently the binding problem.

Should activation ever be a target? The operating camp says yes — an unowned metric is an ignored metric, and Goodhart risk is managed by auditing the correlation. The purist camp says no: a marker decays the moment it becomes a target, so the target should be retention, with activation reported alongside. Prajwalan's five quarters are the purist exhibit; the operating camp answers that its failure was an absent audit, not a property of targets.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this can run the split and quote the lift. Someone who has internalised it asks for coverage before lift, because the ratio alone cannot be interpreted; asks what happened to users who died inside the window before accepting any gap as real; distinguishes "activated users retain better" from "moving a user to activate improves their retention," refusing to let a plan be sized on the first when it depends on the second; and treats the definition as having an expiry date, tracking the correlation rather than the rate.

There is a fifth, less technical marker. An expert can say which of the three jobs the definition is doing this quarter — marker, lever or contract — and will knowingly accept a statistically inferior definition when the binding constraint is coordination rather than prediction, saying plainly that is the trade.

12. The decisions, and three questions

On 22 September, Nandita Rau took the board a plan built on the CACE rather than the observed gap: ₹2.4 crore instead of ₹6.2 crore, aimed at the pairing-first flow the experiment had validated, forecasting 1.1 to 1.6 points of ninety-day retention rather than three. She also put the shipped-but-never-paired cohort on a board slide for the first time, as a larger opportunity than anything in the app and one belonging to channel operations. The smaller ask was approved; the shadow cohort became a workstream with its own owner.

Ira Vaidyanathan gave her investor a different answer from the one requested. She reported the inherited 78 per cent seat-level figure, stated that its explained-variance index was 2.3 and it was not fit for purpose, and supplied an account-level definition — three or more distinct users each with an accepted revision in two separate sessions within thirty days — covering 31 per cent of accounts and predicting renewal far better. She declined to set an activation OKR, proposing instead quarterly reporting of the number with its correlation, and no compensation on it until an encouragement test had sized the lever. Whether the investor would read that as rigour or as absent growth discipline was, she conceded, uncertain.

Discussion questions. First: Prajwalan's activation rate rose from 44 to 67 per cent while its correlation with retention fell from 0.31 to 0.12. When, if ever, is that defensible rather than a failure? Second: Sphuling's causal effect is 44 per cent of its observational gap. What would you need to observe to conclude the rest is selection rather than a weak or badly targeted experiment? Third: what organisational arrangement lets a growth team reach Chingaara's conclusion, the one least favourable to its own budget?

13. Going deeper

  • Constructing a funnel — supplies the candidate events and fixes the denominator, deciding whether the rate measures the product or the traffic.
  • Acquisition, retention, monetisation actions — separates candidate actions from outcomes in disguise, as with Sphuling's subscription event.
  • Cohort analysis — tests whether a definition still predicts what it once did; the only way to see the decay in Fig. 3.
  • Activation and onboarding optimisation — turns a validated definition into a redesigned first hour, where the observational-causal distinction is tested.
  • Reading drop-off — shows where inside the window users are lost, turning "activation is 29 per cent" into a build decision.
  • Retention curves and the PMF signal — supplies the outcome variable, without which activation has no criterion.
  • Stickiness and natural frequency — decides whether a short window is legitimate at all; the intensity camp's strongest argument.
  • Feature adoption analysis — the same statistics after activation, and the guard against mistaking a popular feature for a value moment.
  • Segmenting users in analytics — the channel and liquidity-tier cuts that decide whether one definition suffices.
  • Root cause analysis of a metric change — the drill for section 9: telling a mix shift and an instrumentation break apart from real behaviour.
